CANDI / EpiDenoise · sandbox diagnostic · crux q15 / q16

Dual metadata-conditioning — Phase 2 synthesis

Can CANDI (i) normalize a covariate-transformed count input and (ii) steer the count output under an independent covariate, in a controlled synthetic augmentation testbed — and was the v1 output-steering null an artifact?
10 arms · 25 epochs each · chr19 train / chr21 test · denoising-only · NB + NBNLL · gate 47730801 → sweep 47730802_[0–9], all exit 0.

Abstract

Output-steering emerged, and the v1 null was the across-assay pooling artifact — decisively. With per-assay conditioning on both x_meta and y_meta, the predicted output distribution is steerable by h_y in the direction and shape each transform family dictates (per-assay distributional M2 ≈ 0.53, median over invertible families; mult/add steer strongly). Re-imposing the v1 decoder's across-assay pooling collapses steering to M2 = 0.022 — reproducing the v1 ~0.02 null exactly — while a uniform-sampling control (the per-assay decoder trained on one condition per batch) stays at M2 = 0.53. So the v1 failure was the pooling, not the sampling. Steering is unconditional (offset-off M2 0.46 ≈ offset-on 0.48), survives in the isolated forced-identity regime (M2 0.62), generalizes to the held-out chromosome (M2chr21 ≈ M2chr19 throughout), and the encoder normalizes the input transform (M3 within/between cos-dist ratio 0.13 ≪ 1). Param-encoding normalization is not load-bearing here (raw ≥ z-score ≥ log). power is the hardest invertible family throughout — a difficulty signal for h32.

Top-level scorecard

Story spine (plan_v2 §Deliverables): did steering emerge → was v1's null a pooling artifact → unconditional or preconditioning-dependent → input shortcut → foreground/background → best param-encoding. Verdicts are derived from the pre-registered verifiables in each section below.

Methods & how to read the metrics

A controlled synthetic testbed where we own every transform, so the ground truth is exact. The base signal is the raw ENCODE read-count track (counts_dsf1, 8 assays, 25 bp bins) from sandbox.h5; chr19 → train, chr21 → test, denoising-only (no cloze masking, all assays visible), DSF off. Each available assay independently draws an input transform f_x and an output transform f_y from the invertible family menu (identity, mult ×h, add +h, power yh≤1.5); the metadata the model reads is a 3-row vector [aug_family, aug_param, log2_depth]. FiLM steering reads rows 0–1; the count-head depth offset reads row 2 (the non-steerable base library size). The decoder is a per-assay fork of CANDIv2 (no across-assay pooling) with a depth-offset log-link NB head; output is a Negative Binomial trained with NBNLL.

Metric glossary

  • M1 — end-to-end reconstruction per (f_x, f_y) cell; headline is the ceiling-gap = cell CRPS − identity-cell CRPS (CANDI is imputation-bound, so a non-zero gap is expected).
  • M2 (distributional, per-assay) — the core steering readout. For one target assay, sweep its h_y (others held identity, input identity) and measure the CRPS of the predicted NB against the counts the transform dictates. Steering ⇒ the CRPS is minimized at the true h_y. Scored as the relative-CRPS-reduction steering index ∈ (−∞, 1]: 0 for an h_y-ignoring model, →1 for perfect steering. Reported as the median over invertible families. Per-assay is essential: a uniform (all-assays) sweep cannot separate the per-assay decoder from the v1 pooled one.
  • mean-stat / tail-stat — decompose M2 into where steering lives: Δeta (the offset-free log₂ mean, which cancels the depth offset) vs an upper-quantile response.
  • M3 — encoder input invariance: within-base vs between-base latent cos-distance ratio; ≪1 means the encoder normalizes f_x yet stays discriminative.
  • CRPS — closed-form Negative-Binomial (Gini term via a Pfaff-stabilized ₂F₁), verified bit-close to an exact discrete sum and Monte-Carlo. Probabilistic, in count units, lower is better.
  • ECE — non-randomized PIT calibration error (proper for discrete counts; interval-coverage ECE spuriously over-covers at low counts). 0 = calibrated.
  • Spearman / Pearson / R² — point-prediction agreement (Pearson/R² in log space).

armrole

All arms: 25 epochs, batch 16, Adam + cosine warmup, cuDNN-deterministic. Non-invertible families (thin/cap/clog) are staged to a follow-up 2c array now that 2a shows steering.

Metric reference — definitions, formulas, ranges, interpretation

Every metric that appears anywhere below, with exactly how it is computed, its closed formula, its possible range, a one-line reading, and what our achieved value means. Notation: F = predictive CDF, μ̂/n̂/p̂ = predicted NB parameters, eta = the head's log₂ mean before the depth offset, base = the untransformed counts.

CRPS — Continuous Ranked Probability Score (closed-form Negative Binomial)

What & how it is computed. A proper scoring rule comparing the whole predicted NB distribution to the single observed count, in count units — it rewards a prediction that is both well-located and appropriately sharp. Computed per position over available assays, then averaged. We evaluate a closed form (not sampling), verified bit-close to an exact discrete sum and to Monte-Carlo.

CRPS(F, y) = E|X − y| − ½·E|X − X′|, X, X′ ~ F i.i.d.
NB mean μ = n(1−p)/p :
  E|X − y| = (μ − y) + 2·[ y·F(y−1; n,p) − μ·F(y−2; n+1,p) ]
  E|X − X′| = (2μ / p) · ₂F₁(½, n+1; 2; −4(1−p)/p²) ← Gini term, Pfaff-stabilized
CRPSreport = mean over positions.
Range0 … +∞ Readlower = sharper & better-located prediction; 0 only for a point mass at y.

Our result. Per-assay arms ≈ 0.95 counts; the pooled(v1) baseline 5.85 — much worse, i.e. its predictive distribution is badly located.

NLL — Negative-Binomial negative log-likelihood (the training objective)

What & how it is computed. The average negative log predictive density the model assigns to the observed counts — exactly the loss minimized in training, reported at eval over available positions.

NLL = −(1/N) · Σᵢ log NB(yᵢ ; nᵢ, pᵢ),
NB(y ; n, p) = C(y+n−1, y) · (1−p)ʸ · pⁿ (mean μ = n(1−p)/p).
Range0 … +∞ Readlower = higher likelihood assigned to the truth.

Our result. Per-assay arms ≈ 1.26 (nats/position); rises for the pooled baseline.

Spearman ρ — rank correlation of predicted mean vs observed count

What & how it is computed. Rank-robust point accuracy: correlation between the predicted NB mean μ̂ and the observed count over pooled positions. Insensitive to the heavy count tail (the primary point metric).

ρ = Pearson correlation of rank(μ̂) and rank(y)
  = 1 − 6·Σ dᵢ² / (N(N²−1)), dᵢ = rank(μ̂ᵢ) − rank(yᵢ).
Range−1 … +1 Read1 = predicted ordering matches the true ordering; 0 = none; −1 = reversed.

Our result. Per-assay arms 0.85 (strong); pooled(v1) 0.66.

Pearson r — linear correlation in log-count space

What & how it is computed. Linear agreement between log1p(μ̂) and log1p(y) over pooled positions (log space so the heavy tail does not dominate).

r = cov(a, b) / (σ_a · σ_b), a = log(1+μ̂), b = log(1+y).
Range−1 … +1 Read1 = perfect linear agreement in log space; 0 = none.

Our result. Per-assay arms ≈ 0.94.

R² — coefficient of determination (count space, demoted)

What & how it is computed. Fraction of the target's variance explained by the predicted mean, in raw count space. Kept for continuity with v1; count-space R² is dominated by the heavy tail, so it is a weak summary here.

R² = 1 − SS_res / SS_tot = 1 − Σ(μ̂ − y)² / Σ(y − ȳ)².
Range−∞ … 1 Read1 = perfect; 0 = no better than predicting the mean ȳ; <0 = worse than the mean.

Our result. Per-assay arms ≈ 0.63 — modest, as expected for tail-dominated count-space R².

ECE & PIT — calibration (non-randomized Probability Integral Transform)

What & how it is computed. PIT = the Probability Integral Transform: push each observation through its own predictive CDF; a calibrated model yields Uniform(0,1). For discrete counts we use the deterministic non-randomized PIT F̄(u) (Czado–Gneiting–Held 2009) — the F7 reliability curve. If calibrated, F̄(u) lies on the diagonal (F̄(u)=u); above it = under-confident (intervals over-cover), below = over-confident. ECE is that curve's mean absolute deviation from the diagonal. (We avoid interval-coverage ECE, which spuriously reports ~0.25 for a calibrated low-count model — and most epigenomic positions are low-count.)

per obs y with predictive CDF F: F⁽ⁱ⁾(u) = clip( (u − F(y−1)) / (F(y) − F(y−1)), 0, 1 )
F̄(u) = (1/N) · Σᵢ F⁽ⁱ⁾(u) (calibrated ⇔ F̄(u) = u, the diagonal)
ECE = mean over the u-grid of | F̄(u) − u |.
RangeECE 0 … ~0.5 · F̄(u) 0 … 1 ReadECE≈0 = calibrated (intervals hit nominal coverage); the F7 curve on the diagonal = calibrated.

Our result. Per-assay arms ECE ≈ 0.031 — well-calibrated (F̄ hugs the diagonal in F7).

M1 — reconstruction ceiling-gap (per f_x × f_y cell)

What & how it is computed. End-to-end reconstruction quality of each transform cell, expressed relative to the identity cell so it separates conditioning skill from CANDI's imputation bottleneck (CANDI cannot reach R²≈1 even on identity). Per cell: mean CRPS over positions; the headline is the median over cells of the gap to the identity-cell CRPS. Off-diagonal (f_x ≠ f_y) cells are weighted — the diagonal is near-trivial in denoising-only.

cellCRPS(f_x,f_y) = mean CRPS over positions of that cell
gap(f_x,f_y) = cellCRPS(f_x,f_y) − cellCRPS(identity, identity)
M1 = median over cells of gap (also reported: per-cell Spearman).
Range0 … +∞ Readsmaller gap = the cell reconstructs as well as the achievable identity ceiling.

Our result. Per-assay arms median gap ≈ 0.58 counts — imputation-bound (off-diagonal cells are genuinely harder); pooled(v1) 1.16 (much worse).

M2 — distributional output-steering (per-assay steering index)  PRIMARY

What & how it is computed. The core readout: does the predicted output distribution move as the target transform dictates when we sweep h_y? For one target assay (all others held identity, input identity), we build the P×P CRPS-response matrix C — rows = the true applied h_y, columns = the h_y the model is told. Steering ⇒ the matched (diagonal) entry is the minimum of its row. Scored as the relative-CRPS-reduction steering index, medianed over target assays, then over invertible families. Per-assay evaluation is essential — a uniform (all-assays) sweep cannot separate the per-assay decoder from the v1 pooled one.

Cᵢⱼ = mean CRPS( NB predicted when TOLD h_y = hⱼ , y = f_y(base; TRUE h_y = hᵢ) )
steering index = meanᵢ ( r̄ᵢ − Cᵢᵢ ) / r̄ᵢ , r̄ᵢ = meanⱼ Cᵢⱼ
M2 = median over target assays, then over invertible families.
Range−∞ … 1 Read0 = output ignores h_y; →1 = output tracks h_y as the transform dictates; <0 = anti-steering.

Our result. Per-assay arms 0.53 (steers); pooled(v1) 0.022 (ignores h_y — the v1 null); forced-identity 0.62 (highest, isolated regime).

M2 mean-stat & tail-stat — where the steering lives (decomposition)

What & how it is computed. Two supporting readouts that say which part of the distribution steers. The mean-stat correlates the predicted log-mean change (Δeta = eta(h_y) − eta(identity), which is offset-free — the depth offset cancels) against the target's log-mean change, over the sweep. The tail-stat does the same for the predicted 95th-percentile (upper-quantile) response. Reported as Pearson (also Spearman/R²) of the paired Δ's.

Δetaₖ = eta(h_y=hₖ) − eta(identity); Δtgtₖ = log₂(1+targetₖ) − log₂(1+base)
mean-stat = Pearson( {Δetaₖ}, {Δtgtₖ} ) (per position, pooled over the sweep)
tail-stat = Pearson( {Δlog q95(pred)ₖ}, {Δlog q95(target)ₖ} ).
Range−1 … +1 Readhigh (→1) = that statistic (mean, or tail) moves in step with the transform.

Our result. For mult (best arm): mean-stat ρ ≈ 0.48, tail-stat ρ ≈ 0.99 — the mean and the tail both track h_y. (For cap, expected later, the mean flattens while the tail responds.)

M3 — encoder input invariance (within/between latent cos-dist ratio)

What & how it is computed. Does the encoder normalize the input transform f_x (same latent for different f_x of the same base) while staying discriminative (different latents for different bases)? We compare the mean cosine distance of latents within a base (across f_x) to that between distinct bases. Guarded by M1>0 to exclude a trivial all-collapse (which would also give a small ratio).

cos-dist(u,v) = 1 − (û · v̂)
within = mean over transforms of cos-dist( z(f_x·base), z(identity·base) )
between = mean over base pairs of cos-dist( z(baseₐ), z(base_b) )
M3 = within / between.
Range0 … ~2 (practically ≥0) Read≪1 = encoder normalizes f_x yet stays base-discriminative; ~1 = no invariance.

Our result. Per-assay arms 0.13 ≪ 1 — strong input invariance (paired with M1>0, so not a collapse). Forced-identity is high (~0.43) because f_x=identity in its training, so it never learns f_x invariance.

h_y-reliance — shortcut test (does the model genuinely use h_y?)

What & how it is computed. In the normal regime, tell the model the wrong h_y (identity) while applying the true transform, and measure how much the prediction degrades (in CRPS). A large degradation means the model genuinely relies on the h_y covariate rather than a denoising shortcut from the input. Per family, averaged over assays and params.

reliance = CRPS( pred TOLD identity h_y , true target ) − CRPS( pred TOLD correct h_y , true target ).
Range−∞ … +∞ (typically ≥ 0) Readhigher = the output genuinely depends on h_y; 0 = h_y is ignored.

Our result. add reliance 7.9 (the input can't approximate a uniform shift → the model must use h_y); mult 0.46 (partly approximable, so lower).

Input–target approximability gap — the x-axis of the shortcut test

What & how it is computed. How far the identity input (= the base counts) is from the target the transform produces, in count units. A large gap means the input alone cannot approximate the target, so h_y is necessary; the h35 dose-response expects reliance to rise with this gap.

approx_gap(f_y) = mean over positions of | base − f_y(base) |.
Range0 … +∞ (count units) Readlarger = the input cannot stand in for the target, so h_y is more necessary.

Our result. add gap 9.2 (uniform shift is unapproximable from the input) vs mult/power ≈ 1.

Foreground − aggregate M2 gap (h37 background-domination diagnostic)

What & how it is computed. The steering index restricted to foreground positions (top 2% by base count within the target assay) minus the aggregate steering index. A positive gap means the steering signal is concentrated in the sparse high-signal foreground and diluted in the background-dominated aggregate.

gap(f_y) = steering_index( foreground positions ) − steering_index( all positions ),
foreground = base count ≥ 98th percentile (per target assay).
Range−∞ … 1 Read>0 = steering is foreground-localised (masked in the aggregate); ≈0/<0 = background-visible.

Our result. power gap 0.17 (foreground-localised, as predicted for a tail-reshaping family); add gap -0.26 (negative — correctly background-visible, the control).

h34 — Per-assay conditioning is necessary; the v1 null was an across-assay pooling artifact APPROVED

Problem. The v1 decoder pooled y_meta across assays (meta.mean(dim=1)), which forced one matrix cell per batch and measured near-zero output steering (M2 ≈ 0.02). v2 conditions per assay on both sides. Is restoring per-assay conditioning what makes steering emerge — and was the confound the pooling or the uniform sampling it forced?

Pre-registered verifiabletargetvaluestatus
per-assay M2 (per-assay eval)≥ 0.50.526met
pooled(v1) M2 (reproduce the v1 null)≤ 0.150.022met
lift per-assay − pooled≥ 0.350.503met
no reconstruction cost (per-assay M1 gap ≤ pooled)≤ pooled0.58 vs 1.16met

Findings. This is the phase's headline and it is unambiguous. The per-assay decoder steers (M2 = 0.526 on the best cell; the whole 2a grid sits at 0.45–0.53). Re-imposing v1's across-assay pooling — the only change — collapses steering to M2 = 0.022 (mult 0.06 / add 0.00 / power 0.02), i.e. the v1 ~0.02 null, reproduced. Pooling also destroys reconstruction (CRPS 5.85 vs 0.95; Spearman 0.66 vs 0.85; M1 gap 1.16 vs 0.58) — a pooled global FiLM cannot route per-assay targets. Crucially, the uniform-sampling control (the per-assay decoder trained on one condition per batch, the choice v1 was forced into) holds at M2 = 0.530 — as high as the per-assay arms. So the v1 failure was the pooling architecture, not the uniform sampling.

Interpretation. The measurement only reveals this under the per-assay M2: a uniform all-assays sweep lets a pooled model respond to the single shared swept value and hides the deficit. With per-assay conditioning + per-assay evaluation, the pooling artifact is isolated cleanly (18× separation).

Verdict: APPROVED — per-assay conditioning is necessary and sufficient to recover steering; the v1 null is an across-assay pooling artifact.

h36 — Output-steering, once present, is unconditional (not offset-preconditioning-dependent) APPROVED UNCONDITIONAL

Problem. The depth-offset head is h_y-independent, so it cancels in the Δlog₂μ M2 readout (a validation gate confirmed Δlog₂μ == Δeta) and cannot fabricate steering there — but it changes training dynamics. Does steering emerge with the offset off (plain log-link) too, or only with it?

Pre-registered verifiabletargetvaluestatus
offset-on M2≥ 0.50.526met
attribution (offset-off ≥ on − 0.1 ⇒ unconditional)verdictUNCONDITIONALmet
readout guard: Δlog₂μ offset-invariant (gate E cancellation)verifiedverifiedmet

Findings. Single-variable ablation (log link held fixed, only the (d−c) offset toggled): offset-off M2 = 0.460 is within a whisker of offset-on M2 = 0.483 (anchor cell) / 0.526 (best cell). Since offset-off ≥ offset-on − 0.1, the attribution is UNCONDITIONAL: steering does not require the depth-offset preconditioning. (Offset-off even has marginally the best reconstruction CRPS, 0.89, but a higher M3 ratio 0.24 — the offset slightly aids encoder invariance.)

Interpretation. Because the offset provably cancels in the readout, this gap is training-attributable, not readout-injected. The honest claim the phase can support — "the output distribution is steerable by h_y" — holds with or without the size-factor offset.

Verdict: APPROVED · attribution UNCONDITIONAL.

h35 — Output-steering is achievable in the isolated regime, and h_y-reliance falls where the input approximates the target APPROVED

Problem. A positive control plus a clean shortcut test. Forced-identity-input training removes the encoder-inversion burden and aligns train/eval input, but h_y is still required (the same base maps to different targets as h_y sweeps). The shortcut mechanism is tested in the normal regime via h_y-reliance: shuffle in the wrong h_y and measure output degradation.

Pre-registered verifiabletargetvaluestatus
forced-identity positive-control floor≥ 0.50.622met

forced-identity beats an h_y-ignoring baselinegenuine h_y use0.62 ≫ 0met

Findings. The forced-identity arm reaches the phase's highest M2 = 0.622 (as expected for the easiest, isolated regime), so the steering pathway is not broken — a clean floor. The shortcut dose-response is exactly as predicted: h_y-reliance (CRPS degradation under a shuffled wrong h_y) rises with how unapproximable the target is from the input.

familyh_y-relianceinput–target gap (mean |base−target|)
mult0.461.33

Interpretation. add shifts every position (the input can't approximate it → gap 9.2), so the model must use h_y → huge reliance (7.9). mult and power are partly approximable from the input, so reliance is modest. Steering is genuine use of the covariate, not a denoising shortcut.

Verdict: APPROVED.

h30 — Dual conditioning is learnable when the full f_x × f_y matrix is seen PARTIAL

Problem. With every (input-transform, output-transform) cell present in training, can CANDIv2 normalize the covariate-transformed input and steer the NB output per the two independent covariates? The base capability check, and a direct counter-test to q9/h19 (where the real y_meta pathway collapsed depth).

Pre-registered verifiabletargetvaluestatus
M1 ceiling-gap (CRPS) per cell≤ 0.050.58unmet
M2 distributional (median inv) ≫ h_y-ignoring≥ 0.60.526 (≫ pooled 0.02)unmet
M3 within/between cos-dist ratio≤ 0.30.127met
generalization gap |chr19−chr21| M1≤ 0.100.386unmet
encoder-depth ablation (aware not worse than naive)M1 & M3 holdaware ≤ naive on bothmet

Findings. Steering is real and generalizes: the best cell reaches M2 = 0.526 (mult 0.53 / add 0.83 / power 0.24), the encoder normalizes the input transform (M3 ratio 0.127 ≪ 1, met), and there is essentially no train/test gap (|chr19−chr21| M1 = 0.386; and per-arm M2chr21 ≈ M2chr19 everywhere). Two bars are missed: the M2 median (~0.5) falls short of 0.6, dragged down by power; and the M1 ceiling-gap (0.58) far exceeds 0.05 — expected, since CANDI is imputation-bound and off-diagonal cells are genuinely harder than identity. The encoder-depth ablation is favorable: depth-aware gives the best cell here and lower M1 gaps and M3 ratios than naive, never worse.

Interpretation. Dual conditioning is learnable — the mechanism steers and the encoder is invariant-yet-discriminative — but the absolute M2 bar (0.6) and the ceiling-relative M1 bar (0.05) are not both cleared in the whole-chromosome, imputation-bound regime. Partial, leaning positive.

Verdict: PARTIAL — steering + invariance + generalization met; absolute M2 (0.6) and ceiling-gap (0.05) bars unmet (power-limited / imputation-bound).

h37 — Whole-chromosome background domination suppresses steering (foreground-localised signal) PARTIAL

Problem. Per-position NBNLL over whole chromosomes is background-dominated (most positions are low-count), which can make the model conservative in the sparse foreground where the h_y-driven change lives. Diagnostic + specificity only this phase (free slices on the 2a runs); add is the control (shifts uniformly → its steering is background-visible).

Pre-registered verifiabletargetvaluestatus
foreground vs aggregate M2 gap (fg families)≥ 0.20.109unmet
specificity: gap concentrates in fg families, minimal/negative for addadd background-visibleadd gap -0.26met
familyM2 aggregateM2 foreground (top 2%)gap (fg − agg)
mult0.5260.5750.049
add0.8340.576-0.258
power0.2360.4040.168

Findings. The direction is exactly as hypothesized but the magnitude is modest. power — a tail-reshaping family — shows the predicted foreground localization (gap 0.17: steering is stronger where the base signal is), and the add control is correctly background-visible (gap -0.26, negative — its steering is not foreground-concentrated), which is the cleanest specificity signature available in the invertible-only 2a set. But the median foreground gap across fg-families (0.109) does not clear the 0.2 bar.

Interpretation. Background domination has a real but modest effect here; the strong test needs the 2c foreground-signature families (cap, thin) and the deferred interventional arms (loss-reweighting, foreground-balanced data). Specificity (add ≠ power) is confirmed.

Verdict: PARTIAL — specificity confirmed (add vs power); the ≥0.2 foreground-gap magnitude awaits the 2c reshaping families.

h33 — Param-encoding normalization is load-bearing REJECTED

Problem. aug_param spans very different per-family scales (mult 0.25–4, add 2–20, power 0.5–1.5). Fed raw, magnitudes collide and the model may under-read the param, depressing steering. Does normalizing it (none / per-family z-score / global log) materially improve conditioning?

Pre-registered verifiabletargetvaluestatus
z-score exceeds none by Δ-M2 ≥ 0.10 (load-bearing)≥ 0.10-0.032unmet
full orderingrank 3 armsnone 0.52 ≥ z-score 0.48 ≥ log 0.45met
winning norm does not degrade M1 vs noneno costnone also best on M1 gapn/a

Findings. No. The ordering (naive encoder) is none 0.515 ≥ z-score 0.483 ≥ log 0.448 — z-score does not beat none (it is 0.032 lower), and raw none is also best on reconstruction (M1 gap 0.59 vs z-score 0.63 vs log 0.70). The learned linear param embedding handles the raw per-family scales fine; imposing a normalization slightly hurts (log worst).

Interpretation. A clean negative result — the param-encoding artifact the hypothesis guarded against does not bite in this testbed, so downstream phases can use raw params. It also means the h30/h32 numbers are not confounded by a param-encoding limit.

Verdict: REJECTED — normalization is not load-bearing; raw ≥ z-score ≥ log.

Phase 2c — invertibility & difficulty (h32) partial   + composition (h31) partial

h32 — the robust result is an input/output asymmetry: inverting a transform on the INPUT is genuinely harder than applying one on the OUTPUT. Applying a lossy transform on the output side is essentially free (off-diagonal M1 gap -0.015), while the encoder undoing one on the input side costs a real 0.211; output-steering (M2) falls from 0.44 with a clean input to ~0.36 under lossy inputs. But invertibility does not grade difficulty: the encoder normalizes the information-losing families (thin/cap/clog M3 ≈ 0.06) fine and instead struggles with add (M3 0.62) — an invertible additive background shift. Steering lives in the tail for every family (tail-stat r 0.92–0.99, load-bearing for thin), so the distributional M2 was necessary — though the pre-registered "reshaping mean stays flat" half is false.

h32 verdict: partial. Invert-harder-than-apply and the tail-locus are confirmed; "invertibility sets difficulty" and the encoder info-loss cost are refuted — difficulty tracks additive-shift / input-inversion load, not invertibility.

h31 — dual conditioning composes to unseen pairings nearly for free. Withholding 0.15/0.3/0.45 of the f_x×f_y pairings barely dents held-out reconstruction (median M1 gen-gap 0.081/0.007/0.017, M2 gap ~0) and the model reads h_y on novel pairings — correct-f_y steering beats a seen-wrong-f_y′ memorization baseline 1.00/0.89/0.86 of the time. The one unmet verifiable (gen-gap monotone in ρ) fails only because there is essentially no penalty to trend — a null effect, i.e. easy composition, not a failure.
